chapters.title: Chapter 4: Building a Simple Pairs Trade

lessons.title: Position Sizing and Hedge Ratios: Making the Trade Actually Market-Neutral

children.text: Lesson 6 gave you a hedge ratio, β, out of a regression. Lesson 14 gave you a precise rule for when to enter and exit based on a z-score. Neither one tells a trader sitting at a broker terminal the only question that actually matters at the moment of execution: how many shares of each stock do I actually buy and sell? Get this step wrong, and a statistically sound pair can end up trading like a directional bet in disguise.

body.text: The hedge ratio β from Lesson 6 isn't just a regression statistic. It directly tells you the share ratio needed between the two legs to make the position neutral to their shared historical driver, and that number is often meaningfully different from simply matching rupee value on both sides.

children.text: Recall the regression from Lesson 6: Y = α + βX, meaning a ₹1 move in X has historically come with a ₹β move in Y. For a combined position, long some shares of Y and short some shares of X, to be neutral to that shared driver, a move in X has to affect both legs by roughly equal and opposite amounts. That only happens when the number of shares held in X equals β times the number of shares held in Y.

body.caption: This is the direct, practical translation of Lesson 6's hedge ratio into an actual position. It is not a separate calculation from β, it is the same number, applied to share quantities instead of prices.

children.text: Worked Example: Sizing an HDFC / ICICI Pairs Trade
Continuing Lesson 6's numbers, β ≈ 1.39, with ICICI Bank at ₹1,000 and HDFC Bank at ₹1,599, suppose a trader wants to deploy roughly ₹10 lakh in this pair.

body.code:
icici_price = 1000
hdfc_price = 1599
beta = 1.39
target_capital = 1_000_000

cost_per_unit = hdfc_price + beta * icici_price
n_hdfc = round(target_capital / cost_per_unit)
n_icici = round(n_hdfc * beta)

print("HDFC shares:", n_hdfc)
print("ICICI shares (hedge-ratio-implied):", n_icici)
print("Total capital deployed:", n_hdfc * hdfc_price + n_icici * icici_price)
# HDFC shares: 335
# ICICI shares (hedge-ratio-implied): 466
# Total capital deployed: 1001665
body.caption: Solving for whole-share quantities that respect the β = 1.39 hedge ratio, targeting about ₹10 lakh total

children.text: The Trap: "Equal Rupee Value on Both Legs" Is Not the Same Thing

markDefs.definition: Sizing the two legs of a trade so their rupee values are equal. A common simplification, but not the same thing as being hedged against the pair's estimated historical relationship.

children.text: A common shortcut is to size both legs to the same rupee value, so-called

sizing. With 335 HDFC shares worth ₹5,35,665, matching that exact rupee value on the ICICI leg would mean buying 536 ICICI shares (₹5,35,665 ÷ ₹1,000, rounded). That is a genuinely different number from the 466 shares the actual hedge ratio calls for, about 15% more shares than the pair's estimated historical relationship justifies.

body.text: Dollar-neutral sizing implicitly assumes a 1:1 rupee-for-rupee relationship between the two stocks, which is really just their raw price ratio (about 1.6 here). The regression hedge ratio, 1.39, is a different, more carefully estimated number, and using the wrong one leaves the position with real, uncancelled exposure to whatever moves both stocks together, exactly what the hedge ratio was supposed to remove.

children.text: β is a decimal. Shares, and in the F&O segment, lots, are not. The theoretical ICICI quantity here was 465.65 shares (335 × 1.39), rounded up to 466 whole shares. That rounding is unavoidable, and it leaves a small residual exposure that the hedge ratio didn't quite fully cancel.

body.label: Rounding residual on the ICICI leg
body.context: 466 whole shares vs the theoretical 465.65 implied by β × 335, about 0.07% of the HDFC leg's value here. Negligible at this size, but proportionally larger for very small positions, another reason not to size a pairs trade too thin.

children.text: How Much Capital to Put in One Pair

Even a pair that passes every test in Chapters 2 and 3 still carries real risk, the structural break risk from Lesson 4, the stop-loss scenarios from Lesson 14, and the corporate action risk Lesson 12 flagged for commonly-owned pairs. No single pair, however well tested, should absorb all of a trader's capital. Chapter 7 covers running several pairs together for genuine diversification. There is also a real capital cost specific to the short leg: exchange margin requirements, SPAN and exposure margin on an F&O short position, mean the capital actually locked up is more than just the notional position value shown in the table above, a detail that matters for how many pairs a given amount of capital can actually support at once.

body.title: Apply the hedge ratio to a new pair
body.prompt: A different pair has a fitted hedge ratio of β = 0.65 (from regressing Y on X). If you hold 500 shares of Y, how many shares of X does the hedge ratio imply you should hold on the opposite side?
body.explanation: shares of X = β × shares of Y = 0.65 × 500 = 325.

body.title: Why doesn't "equal rupee value" work?
body.question: In this lesson's HDFC/ICICI example, a dollar-neutral approach implied 536 ICICI shares, while the regression hedge ratio implied only 466 ICICI shares for the same 335 HDFC shares. Why do these differ?
options: One of the two calculations must contain an arithmetic error

Dollar-neutral sizing assumes the two stocks move rupee-for-rupee in a 1:1 relationship, while the regression hedge ratio uses the two stocks' actual estimated historical sensitivity to each other, a different number
ICICI Bank cannot be shorted, so the dollar-neutral number is not achievable
The hedge ratio only applies to the entry rule, not to position sizing
body.explanation: Dollar-neutral sizing implicitly assumes a 1:1 rupee-for-rupee relationship, which is really just the raw price ratio between the two stocks (about 1.6 here). The regression hedge ratio (β ≈ 1.39) is a different number, estimated directly from how the two prices have actually historically moved together, and is the one that specifically cancels out their shared driver.

cards.definition: Setting the share quantities of the two legs of a pairs trade so that shares of X equal β times shares of Y, matching the regression-estimated hedge ratio from Lesson 6.

Setting the share quantities of the two legs so their rupee values are equal. A common simplification, but not the same thing as being properly hedged against the pair's estimated historical relationship.
The small, unavoidable mismatch between a theoretical hedge ratio (a decimal) and the whole share or lot quantities actually tradeable, leaving a small amount of unhedged exposure.

points: The regression hedge ratio β from Lesson 6 directly implies the share ratio needed between the two legs of a pairs trade: shares of X should equal β times shares of Y, for the position to be neutral to their shared historical driver.

Dollar-neutral sizing, matching equal rupee value on both legs, is a common shortcut but is not the same as hedge-ratio-implied sizing. The two can differ substantially, about 15% in this lesson's worked example.
Because β is a decimal and shares must be whole numbers, or F&O lot multiples, some rounding residual is unavoidable. It is typically small relative to a meaningfully sized position.

Position sizing also has to account for real capital constraints: exchange margin requirements on the short leg, and how much of total trading capital to risk on a single pair rather than spreading it across several.
None of this replaces the entry, exit, and stop-loss discipline from Lesson 14. Correct sizing makes a well-tested pair tradeable; it does not make a poorly tested one safe.
